newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Special economic status for Chechnya mooted.
newsitem.headline: Special economic status for Chechnya mooted.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said on Thursday the war-torn region of Chechnya should have special economic status and that he was ready to meet separatist leaders.
"It is clear that there must be special (economic) conditions there," said Chernomyrdin, cited by Itar-Tass news agency, after chairing a session of Russia's powerful Security Council.
President Boris Yeltsin, who normally chairs meetings of the Security Council, was absent as he is preparing for a heart operation due this week.
Yeltsin sent troops into the northern Caucasus territory in December 1994 to crush a three-year-old bid for independence from the Russian Federation.

Tens of thousands of people were killed and the capital Grozny devastated in a widely-criticised military operation before a ceasefire was negotiated by former presidential security adviser Alexander Lebed in August.
Chernomyrdin said he was ready to meet separatist leaders. "In Chechnya, in Grozny or here (Moscow), wherever's necessary, such a meeting will take place," he said, according to Tass.

Boris Berezovsky, the newly appointed deputy secretary of the Security Council, said in an interview on Russian state television: "Russia will pay any price to establish peace in the Caucasus...and maintain Russia's territorial integrity."
Berezovsky was speaking during a visit to Chechnya -- his first since his appointment -- which focused on financing reconstruction in the republic.
Chernomyrdin said the Security Council should consider a law to make Chechnya a free economic zone, Tass said. It gave no details.
Grozny Mayor Lechi Dudayev met Moscow's own mayor, Yuri Luzhkov, in the Russian capital to discuss economic ties between the two cities, Tass reported.
Dudayev is a nephew of the Chechen separatist leader Dzhokhar Dudayev who was killed in a Russian rocket attack in April.

In establishing the ceasefire the two sides put off tackling the question of whether Chechnya should remain a semi-autonomous ethnic republic within the Russian Federation or become fully independent.
Other political problems remain, including arranging regional elections.
Chernomyrdin said on Monday he did not rule out elections in the territory in January 1997 but underlined the need for security guarantees, Tass said.
